summary: Describes the packet format and forwarding behavior for Source Demand Routing Protocol, which supports source-selected routes to complement what ordinary routing protocols choose. It works for both inter-domain and intra-domain routes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Normally the road signs decide your path. This lets the sender pick their own path through the network instead.

questions: what is the difference between strict and loose source routes
how do sdrp routers forward packets
subtitle: Let a sender specify the exact path packets should take through the network.

tldr.problem: Ordinary routing protocols make routing decisions at each hop, but sometimes a source wants to specify the entire path packets should take, particularly for traffic engineering and specific network paths.
tldr.mechanism: SDRP encapsulates the original IP packet with a header containing a complete domain-level or router-level path specified by the sender, then forwards the packet along this pre-determined route.
tldr.outcome: Packets follow the sender's chosen path instead of the path ordinary routing would select. This enables source control over routing for both inter-domain and intra-domain routes.

today: RFC 1940 is an Informational document that has not been obsoleted or updated. SDRP was proposed for routing control but saw limited deployment, largely superseded by more refined approaches to traffic engineering and policy-based routing in modern Internet backbones.

sections.title: Overview and Purpose
sections.content:
SDRP—Source Demand Routing Protocol—lets a source host or intermediate router choose the exact path that a packet takes through the network. Ordinary routing protocols like BGP decide the path at each hop based on local routing tables. SDRP instead lets the sender specify a sequence of domains or routers that the packet must visit, and the packet is encapsulated and forwarded along that precise route.

The RFC describes the packet format and forwarding behavior for SDRP. The route can mix domain-level hops (specified as Autonomous System numbers) with router-level hops (specified as IP addresses). Hops can be strict (the next hop must be immediately adjacent) or loose (routing protocols find a path to the next hop).
sections.eli5: You give the packet a list of places to visit in order, and every router along the way checks the list and forwards it to the next place on your list.

sections.title: Network Model and Routing Domains
sections.content:
SDRP assumes the Internet is divided into routing domains (autonomous systems) connected by Border Routers. Within each domain, interior routers use intra-domain routing (IGPs). When a packet crosses domain boundaries, it traverses Border Routers that form inter-domain connections.

An SDRP route is a sequence of domains and routers—components called hops. The route is encoded as a list of Domain Identifiers (AS numbers) or IP addresses. Each router in the path checks the next hop and either forwards the packet within its domain, to an adjacent domain, or directly to the next router address.
sections.eli5: The network has big domains connected by special routers. Your route is a list of either domain numbers or router addresses, and packets bounce from one to the next in order.

sections.title: SDRP Packet Format
sections.content:
An SDRP packet wraps the original IP packet inside an SDRP header. The header begins with a version field (set to 1) and control flags that indicate whether the packet carries data, whether the route is strict or loose, and whether the sender is probing the route's feasibility.

The header includes a Hop Count field (like TTL), a Source Route Identifier (for the originating router to track the route), and the route itself—a variable-length field containing the sequence of hops. The next hop pointer indicates which hop the packet is currently trying to reach. Additional fields carry IP address prefixes and notification codes for control packets.

The entire original IP packet is carried as the payload, with the SDRP MTU determining the largest payload that can be sent without fragmentation.
sections.eli5: The SDRP header is like an address label stuck on top of the original packet, with the full route written on it and a pointer showing which stop you are currently at.

sections.title: Forwarding and Route Traversal
sections.content:
When a router receives an SDRP packet, it extracts the next hop from the source route and decides how to forward the packet. The behavior depends on whether the route is strict or loose, whether the next hop is a domain identifier or an IP address, and whether the next hop is the local domain or router.

For domain-level hops, the router consults its D-FIB (domain forwarding information base) to find the next border router. For router-level hops, it forwards directly to that IP address. If a strict hop is not immediately adjacent, the packet is discarded and a control packet signals the error. With loose hops, the router can use standard routing protocols to reach the next hop.

When the route is completely traversed and the packet reaches the destination domain, the SDRP header is removed and the payload is forwarded normally.
sections.eli5: At each stop, the router reads the next entry on the route, figures out how to get there (either directly or using normal routing), and sends the packet onward.

sections.title: Error Handling and Control Packets
sections.content:
If a router cannot forward an SDRP packet—due to a missing route, a failed strict hop, a hop count limit, or a transit policy violation—it generates an SDRP control packet and sends it back to the encapsulating router. The control packet carries a notification code indicating the failure type: No Route Available, Strict Source Route Failed, Transit Policy Violation, Hop Count Exceeded, or Unimplemented SDRP version.

A sender can also request route feasibility checking by setting the Probe Indicator flag. If the packet successfully reaches its destination, the last router generates a Probe Completed control packet. The sender uses these control packets to mark routes as feasible or infeasible and select alternate routes if needed.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, the routers send a message back to the sender explaining what failed. The sender can also ask routers along the way to confirm the route works.

sections.title: MTU Discovery and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
SDRP supports Path MTU Discovery to determine the maximum packet size that can traverse a route without fragmentation. A router can discover the MTU via ICMP Destination Unreachable messages (passive discovery) or by sending probe packets with the Don't Fragment flag set and listening for probe completion responses (active discovery).

The RFC notes that SDRP can initially be deployed with manually configured routes. Future versions are expected to include dynamic route distribution and computation. The document also assumes that Border Routers participate in BGP or IDRP and that routers enforce local transit policies—rules about which source routes are allowed through a domain.
sections.eli5: Routers need to know the biggest packet size that fits on a route. The sender can discover this by sending test packets and listening for responses. In the beginning, network managers will write the routes by hand.

fields.name: Version and Flags
fields.desc: Version (3 bits), Data/Control bit, Strict/Loose bit, Probe bit.

fields.name: Hop Count
fields.desc: Maximum routers to traverse; decremented by each SDRP router.

fields.name: Source Protocol Type
fields.desc: Type of source route (1 = Explicit Source Route).

fields.name: Source Route Identifier
fields.desc: Unique identifier for this route, assigned by originating router.

fields.name: Target Router
fields.desc: IP address of originating router (meaningful in control packets).

fields.name: Prefix
fields.desc: IP address prefix for loop prevention in loose routes.

fields.name: Prefix Length
fields.desc: Number of significant bits in the prefix (0 = all addresses).

fields.name: Notification Code
fields.desc: Error code in control packets; transmitted as zero in data packets.

fields.name: Next Hop Pointer
fields.desc: Offset to current next hop in the source route.
